name: crcany
desc: Compute any CRC, a bit at a time, a byte at a time, and a word at a time
why: A generator for any CRC variant that shows the bit-level machinery behind checksums in a way few people have seen.

brief.what_it_is: crcany is a C suite of programs that compute any CRC from its parameter set (the Greg Cook / Ross Williams model format) and can generate C code for it. It takes a CRC definition, either by catalogue name or as parameters, plus data bytes, and outputs the checksum. It can also combine two CRCs, given the CRC of each sequence and the length of the second, to get the CRC of the concatenation. A companion tool generates .c and .h files for one or many CRC definitions.
brief.why_it_exists: The README's stated motivation is to "Provide once and for all a definitive reference for how to compute and combine any CRC with any of bit, byte, or word-at-a-time algorithms, on any big or little-endian architecture."
brief.how_it_works: It computes a CRC bit at a time, as a hardware shift register would. For byte-at-a-time, it first uses the bit-at-a-time routine to build a 256-entry table of CRCs for all byte values. For word-at-a-time, it expands the byte table into n-1 further tables, where n is the word size in bytes, with separate little-endian and big-endian flavors.

commands_seen.context: Compiles the crcany, crctest, crcall, crcadd, and mincrc executables from the repository root.
Tests CRC calculation and generated CRC code against the full list of catalogued CRCs.

brief.install_notes: Build from source with make; the README names no other dependencies, accounts, or runtimes. Generated code defaults to the host's integer sizes and endianness, and can be forced to 32- or 64-bit words and big- or little-endian. The README gives no usage syntax for the crcany binary itself.
brief.standout: It treats the CRC as a single parameterized algorithm and generates optimized C for any width up to 64 bits, rather than hard-coding one polynomial. It also includes CRC combination, which lets you join checksums of separate blocks without re-reading the data.
brief.status: unknown. The README has no release or version notes and I saw no commit dates. It does have a working build and test target and a full catalogue of CRC definitions.
brief.caveats: The README documents no usage syntax for crcany itself, so anyone writing examples will need to read the source or run it. Code generation is limited to CRCs up to 64 bits; the bit-wise calculation goes up to 128 bits on 64-bit machines. The getcrcs tool scrapes Greg Cook's website for definitions. The README does not name a C compiler requirement or a platform list beyond the endianness discussion.
quotes: _crcany_ can compute a CRC in three different ways.

entry.title: crcany
entry.tldr: Computes and generates C code for any CRC from its parameters, showing the same checksum done bit by bit, byte by byte and word by word.
entry.deeper_look:
crcany is a small C suite that treats a CRC as one parameterized algorithm. You give it a CRC definition in the Greg Cook / Ross Williams parameter model, either by catalogue name or as raw parameters, and it computes the checksum. It can also combine two CRCs: given the CRC of each block and the length of the second, it produces the CRC of the concatenation without re-reading the data. A companion tool writes .c and .h files for one or many CRC definitions.

The interesting part is how the three algorithms relate. The bit-at-a-time version behaves like a hardware shift register. The byte-at-a-time version builds a 256-entry table by running the bit-at-a-time routine on every byte value. The word-at-a-time version expands that table into n-1 more tables, where n is the word size in bytes, with separate little-endian and big-endian flavors.

The README states the goal plainly: "Provide once and for all a definitive reference for how to compute and combine any CRC with any of bit, byte, or word-at-a-time algorithms, on any big or little-endian architecture." It is written by Mark Adler, so it is a reference you can read to see why table-driven CRCs work, not just a tool to run.

The door it opens is the family of CRC variants: why CRC-32 and CRC-16 flavors differ in polynomial, bit order, initial value and final XOR, and how fast implementations are derived from the slow, obvious one.

entry.whats_unique: Rather than hard-coding one polynomial, it generates code for any CRC up to 64 bits in bit, byte and word-at-a-time forms, and includes CRC combination.
entry.caveats: The README documents no usage syntax for the crcany binary, code generation stops at 64 bits, and the brief shows no version or commit dates.
